claims.text: Packed binary byte count is not vector dimensionality: 1024 binary dimensions occupy 128 payload bytes. Preserve the original dimension count in the index; do not set numDimensions to the packed array length. (medium confidence)

When only pre-quantized vectors are ingested, MongoDB does not retain an original full-precision copy for automatic rescoring. MongoDB's tutorial recommends retaining a separate float32 field with automatic binary quantization if that rescoring behavior is required; the extra representation belongs in the storage cost model. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Generate document and query embeddings with the same model and matching vector dimensions. For pre-quantized fields, serialize the query with the matching BinData element type; full-fidelity queries against int8/int1 fields can return no results without an error. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Compared with float32 payload values, scalar int8 uses one quarter of the bytes and packed binary uses one thirty-second. Those arithmetic ratios describe vector values; they do not directly describe total index memory, database storage, or the cluster bill. MongoDB notes that HNSW graph memory does not shrink with the vector values. (medium confidence)

Use driver vector serializers rather than an arbitrary binary blob: the Java example wraps model-returned bytes with BinaryVector.int8Vector(byte[]) or BinaryVector.packedBitVector(byte[], padding). These wrappers tag the vector representation; they do not quantize arbitrary float embeddings. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

For pre-quantized vectors, omit fields.quantization or set it to none. Enabling automatic scalar or binary quantization on int8/int1 BinData can silently skip those vectors instead of indexing them. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

For a consolidation TCO estimate, account separately for smaller stored vector payloads, search-index memory, serialization work in ingestion and queries, and any retained float representation. These sources establish possible resource savings but do not establish a measured Atlas-versus-separate-database TCO advantage. (medium confidence)

Cohere’s Embed API documents int8, uint8, binary, and ubinary outputs alongside floats and permits multiple output types in one request. MongoDB’s available element types still require the application to choose a compatible representation rather than treating every provider dtype as interchangeable. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

MongoDB can ingest and index model-produced int8 and packed int1 vectors stored as BSON BinData. This stores reduced-precision values in mongod itself, whereas automatic index quantization leaves the original document vectors intact. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

BSON vector storage uses binary subtype 9. Its element dtype distinguishes INT8 (0x03), FLOAT32 (0x27), and PACKED_BIT (0x10); a dtype byte and padding byte precede the vector payload. (low confidence)

MongoDB's documented pre-quantized int1 ingestion requires dimensions that are multiples of eight and euclidean similarity. Int8 ingestion supports cosine, euclidean, and dotProduct; both support ANN and ENN. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Cohere provides an upstream producer for quantized ingestion: its Embed API supports explicit int8 and binary/ubinary outputs, and the documentation shows requesting int8 and float together. Provider output must still be serialized into MongoDB's vector format. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Embedding quantization does not preserve retrieval quality uniformly across models. Hugging Face's experiments show model-dependent degradation and stress that scalar calibration ranges affect performance; treating a float-to-int8 cast as equivalent to validated embedding quantization is unsafe. (medium confidence)

The BSON format permits PACKED_BIT padding from zero through seven bits, while non-packed dtypes require zero padding. That general serialization allowance does not override MongoDB Vector Search's documented multiple-of-eight int1 ingestion requirement. (medium confidence)

MongoDB supports ingesting and indexing pre-quantized int8 and int1 embeddings as BSON BinData vectors. Quantization occurs before insertion; supported drivers serialize the reduced-precision output into the vector binary format. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

BSON vector storage uses binary subtype 9. INT8 (dtype 0x03), FLOAT32 (0x27), and PACKED_BIT (0x10, used for int1) are element types within that subtype, not three separate BSON binary subtype numbers. (medium confidence)

An INT8 vector stores signed values in [-128,127]. A PACKED_BIT vector groups binary dimensions into bytes; the BSON specification describes these packed byte values as integers in [0,255]. Scalar int8 elements and bytes that pack eight binary dimensions are different representations. (medium confidence)

MongoDB documents euclidean similarity for int1 ingestion, with dimensions a multiple of eight; int8 ingestion supports cosine, euclidean, and dotProduct. The Java example uses euclidean for its packed-bit field. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

The Java example serializes pre-quantized outputs using BinaryVector.int8Vector(byte[]) and BinaryVector.packedBitVector(byte[], padding). MongoDB’s Python examples use Binary.from_vector with BinaryVectorDtype.INT8 or PACKED_BIT. These helpers encode vectors; they do not by themselves calibrate a float-to-int8 quantizer. (medium confidence)

Pre-quantized document storage can reduce mongod disk and WiredTiger footprint as well as mongot index memory. Automatic index quantization instead retains full-precision document embeddings, so the two approaches have different storage cost implications. (medium confidence)

Client-side scalar quantization needs consistent calibration ranges: Hugging Face explains that per-dimension calibration buckets affect retrieval performance. MongoDB also describes scalar quantization using per-dimension minimum and maximum ranges. Casting arbitrary floats to integer bytes is therefore not equivalent to a calibrated quantization pipeline. (medium confidence)
